newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Russia diamond republic in environment deal.
newsitem.headline: Russia diamond republic in environment deal.

text.p: Russia's diamond-producing Yakutia region signed an accord on Tuesday with the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) to protect Arctic lakes and forests in a quarter of its vast territory three times the size of France.

The Swiss-based environment protection agency will allocate $350,000 to fund conservation projects in the semi-autonomous republic on the rim of the Arctic Circle in Siberia, WWF director general Claude Martin told a news conference.
The remote republic, also known as Sakha, has 600,000 lakes, thousands of rivers and is home to endangered species like polar bears and Siberian cranes.
Yakutia, plundered recklessly in Soviet times to obtain diamonds, oil, gold and minerals lying beneath the snow, cut a deal with Moscow in 1990 for a 20 percent share of its vast diamond reserves.
"Mistakes made in the past have left us with a heritage of severe environmental degradation," Yakut president Mikhail Nikolayev told the news conference. "We want this to change."
The Soviet Union began a mass settlement drive in Yakutia, building entire new towns in the region, packed in ice for two-thirds of the year and among the world's most inhospitable.
The Turkic-speaking republic is covered in permafrost and its climate is so harsh it can take half a century for trees to grow more than head high.
In the 1970s and 1980s, Soviet engineers set off underground nuclear explosions to blast through permafrost and build a dam on ice. They were halted after radiation leaks.
Seven of the 12 "peaceful" underground atomic explosions in Yakutia had a yield equal to or more powerful than that of the bomb dropped on Hiroshima, its officials say.
Dead forests now surround the sites where surface radiation has since faded. But the underground blasts have pumped permafrost with radioctive material.

Diamond and gold processing have filled the Vilyui River with traces of thallium and other highly toxic chemicals. Yet another danger was the second stage of Soviet rockets jettisoned in mid-flight, which kept falling on Yakut territory.
"Instead of trying to conquer nature like we did in the past, now we want to have a mutually beneficial relationship," said Yakutia's environment minister Vasily Alekseyev.
